what_it_does: Approximate logic synthesis is a chip-design technique where you intentionally allow a circuit to occasionally compute slightly wrong answers in exchange for a smaller, faster, or lower-power chip — useful for applications like image processing where a tiny error is invisible to users. Most existing tools optimize for just one goal at a time (make it as small as possible, or make it as fast as possible) while respecting a maximum allowed error, but not both goals simultaneously. This paper applies Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) — the same game-tree search algorithm used in AlphaGo for chess and Go — to explore which small local circuit changes (swapping a logic gate, simplifying a sub-expression) to apply and in what order, while simultaneously trading off multiple objectives. A neural network called Rank-Transformer is trained to predict which candidate changes are most promising, so the search focuses its budget on high-value moves. The multi-objective aspect is handled by ranking candidate circuits using a concept from evolutionary optimization: a circuit is ranked by how many other circuits it is not dominated by (meaning no other circuit beats it on all objectives at once). Based on the abstract, the approach is expected to escape the local optima that plague single-objective methods.
